I took LSD with two friends at a cabin by a lake. My grandmother had been in hospital for a week with pneumonia, but the doctors had said she was stable and that I shouldn't cancel the trip. Around three hours in, at the peak, my phone rang. It was my mother, crying. She said grandma had taken a turn for the worse and might not make it through the night, and that if I wanted to say goodbye I should come now.

I couldn't drive. Nobody could drive. The hospital was four hours away. I stood in the cabin holding the phone and the floor tilted under me. My mother's voice was coming out of the phone in colours, a dark purple, and I couldn't understand what she was saying anymore. I kept saying 'I'm coming, I'm coming' while knowing I couldn't.

After I hung up, I sat on the porch and the lake turned black. I felt my grandmother dying, not as a thought, but physically, like her breathing was in my own chest, slowing down. I saw her face in the water, getting further away. I was sure that I was being shown the exact moment of her death and that she was calling for me and I wasn't there. I felt that I had chosen drugs over my family and that this was the price.

My friends tried to comfort me, but I couldn't bear to be touched. I walked into the forest and sat against a tree, howling. Time stopped. I thought the night would never end and that I'd be stuck forever in the moment of her dying.

At 4am my mother called again. Grandma had died around 2. I was still tripping, though less. I don't remember what I said. At 8am one of my friends was sober enough to drive, and we drove to the hospital in silence. I arrived too late to say goodbye. My mother hugged me and smelled my hair and I think she knew I'd taken something. Nobody said anything.

Ich war mit zwei Freunden in Amsterdam und wir hatten Trüffel aus einem Smartshop gegessen. Danach haben wir Fahrräder gemietet, was im Nachhinein total verrückt war. Ich bin hinter meinen Freunden hergefahren, und plötzlich wurde der Verkehr zu einem einzigen Strom aus Lichtern und Geräuschen. Ich konnte nicht mehr unterscheiden, was nah und was fern ist. An einer Kreuzung bin ich einfach weitergefahren, und eine Straßenbahn kam von links. Ich habe ihr Klingeln gehört, aber es klang wie aus einer anderen Welt. Ich weiß nicht, wie ich ausgewichen bin. Ich bin gestürzt, die Bahn hat etwa einen Meter neben mir gebremst. Der Fahrer hat mich angeschrien, Leute sind stehen geblieben.

Ich lag auf dem Boden und hatte das Gefühl, dass ich gestorben bin und dass das hier die Zeit danach ist. Ich habe meinen Körper nicht gespürt. Ich habe geglaubt, dass mein Körper unter der Bahn liegt und ich nur noch als Geist auf der Straße sitze. Erst als einer meiner Freunde mich angefasst hat, habe ich gemerkt, dass ich noch da bin, und dann habe ich angefangen zu zittern und konnte nicht mehr aufhören. Wir haben die Räder irgendwo stehen lassen und sind zu Fuß ins Hostel. Ich habe die ganze Nacht die Straßenbahn klingeln gehört.

I'm 55. My son died in a motorcycle accident four years ago, and I had been in a deep grief that nothing seemed to touch. A woman in my yoga class told me about a two-day 'women's medicine circle' in the mountains in Spain, with San Pedro cactus, and said it had helped her through her divorce. I went with an open heart and, I see now, with very little information.

There were twelve women and two facilitators. We slept on mats in a stone building with no heating. It was October and the nights were cold. The first evening we drank the cactus brew, which was bitter and made me vomit almost immediately. The facilitators said this was the medicine 'taking what I no longer need'. The effects came on slowly over hours. For a long time I just felt nauseous and very cold.

The circle went on through the night with singing and drumming and each woman sharing. We were encouraged not to sleep, because the medicine 'works best through the night'. In the early morning we were given a second cup. I hadn't slept, I hadn't eaten, and I was shivering. When the second cup took hold, the world changed completely.

I saw my son. He was standing in the doorway in his motorcycle jacket. At first I was overjoyed and I stood up to go to him, but he turned and walked out, and I followed him out into the mountains. I don't remember deciding to leave the building. It was dawn and freezing and I was wearing only a thin dress and a blanket. I walked for what must have been a long time, following him along a rocky path, calling his name. Every time I got close, he disappeared and reappeared further away.

Then he stopped at the edge of a slope and turned to me, and his face was the face from the hospital, broken and grey. I fell to my knees. I understood, in that state, that he had been waiting for me to come with him, and that I should. I felt my body becoming heavy and cold, and it felt right, it felt like the end of four years of pain. I lay down on the stones and closed my eyes. I felt myself dissolving into the mountain, into the cold, and I was not afraid, which in retrospect is the most frightening part.

I don't know how long I lay there. One of the other women had noticed I was gone and the facilitators eventually found me, around two hours later. I was hypothermic and confused. They carried me back and wrapped me in sleeping bags and gave me hot tea. They didn't call a doctor. They said I had gone on 'a deep journey with my son'. One of them told me that he had 'released' me and that I should be grateful.

For the rest of the second day I lay in the corner shaking and drifting in and out of strange states. I wanted to go home and was told that leaving early would 'close the container badly'. I stayed because I couldn't think clearly enough to arrange transport. On the third day a woman from the group drove me to the airport.

I bought blotters from someone I knew, sold as LSD. Later I found out it was most likely DOC, which lasts much longer and is more stimulating. I took one tab at 6pm at home with my girlfriend. It came on slower than LSD, and for the first few hours it seemed fine. Then it just didn't stop. By 3am I was still peaking, my body was buzzing, my jaw ached, my heart was racing. My girlfriend had taken half a tab and fell asleep around 5am. I couldn't. I lay next to her watching the ceiling crawl, unable to close my eyes because when I did I saw spinning machinery.

By noon the next day I was still tripping. I began to panic that I'd taken something that would never wear off. I googled 'LSD lasting 20 hours' and read horror stories about permanent psychosis. The visuals were still strong, everything breathing and rippling. I hadn't eaten, I hadn't slept, my muscles were cramping. By the evening, 24 hours later, it was mostly gone, but the world still looked wrong and I still couldn't sleep. I slept for the first time about 40 hours after taking it.

Ich war mit Freunden an einem Bergsee und hatte LSD genommen. Wir sind geschwommen, und mitten im See bekam ich einen Wadenkrampf. Das Wasser war plötzlich schwarz und tief und ich war mir sicher, dass ich ertrinke. Ich habe geschrien und um mich geschlagen. Ein Freund ist zu mir geschwommen und hat mich ans Ufer gezogen. Am Ufer habe ich stundenlang gezittert und konnte das Bild vom schwarzen Wasser nicht loswerden.

I'm a big gamer, and I had the very stupid idea of trying VR while on LSD. I'd taken about 150ug at home alone and I put on my headset to play a space exploration game. At first it was incredible, the stars, the planets, the sense of floating. I spent maybe two hours in there.

When I took the headset off, my apartment looked fake. It looked like a worse-rendered version of the game. The walls had the same texture problems, edges looked jagged, and when I moved my head, the room seemed to lag a fraction behind. I became convinced that the room was the simulation and the game was real, or that both were simulations and I had no idea which layer I was in.

I put the headset back on to 'check', and then took it off again, and on and on, maybe twenty times. Each time, the boundaries between the two got blurrier. At one point I was in the game and reached out to touch a planet and my hand hit my real desk, and the shock of it made me scream. I felt like my mind had been unplugged from my body.

I ended up sitting in the shower with my clothes on, because the feeling of water was the only thing that felt real. I stayed there until the hot water ran out. I couldn't touch the headset for months.

I was doing at-home ketamine treatment for depression through an online telehealth company. They send you lozenges and you do the session on your own, with a short video call before and after. During my fourth session I took the prescribed dose and lay down with my eyeshade. Something felt different. I left my body and couldn't find my way back. I had the feeling that I was dead and that my body was lying on the bed and no one would find it for days because I live alone. I couldn't move or speak. When it wore off I tried to call the provider's support line and got an automated message.

Ich habe an einer Ayahuasca-Zeremonie teilgenommen, die in einer Privatwohnung im Ruhrgebiet stattfand. Wir waren etwa acht Personen, der Leiter kam aus Südamerika, und es gab eine Helferin. Die Fenster waren verhängt, es gab Kerzen und Matten auf dem Boden.

Die Medizin wirkte sehr stark. Ich hatte Visionen von Jaguaren und einem riesigen Baum, unter dem ich saß. Zunächst war das schön. Dann, etwa zwei Stunden nach Beginn, klingelte es an der Tür, mehrmals, laut. Jemand hämmerte dagegen. Der Leiter stand auf und flüsterte, wir sollten ruhig bleiben. Dann hörte ich Stimmen: Polizei, aufmachen. Ein Nachbar hatte offenbar wegen des Gesangs und eines merkwürdigen Geruchs die Polizei gerufen.

Was danach passierte, war für mich der Horror. Die Polizei kam mit vier Beamten in die Wohnung. Sie machten das Licht an, das grelle Deckenlicht, und verlangten von allen die Ausweise. Ich lag auf meiner Matte und konnte kaum sprechen. Die Visionen gingen weiter, und die Uniformen und Taschenlampen wurden zu Teilen einer Hölle. Ich sah die Polizisten als dunkle, maskierte Gestalten mit glühenden Augen. Eine Teilnehmerin neben mir fing an zu schreien und musste sich übergeben, und ein Beamter hat sie angebrüllt, sie solle aufhören. Ich hatte das Gefühl, dass wir alle hingerichtet werden.

Sie haben die Reste des Getränks beschlagnahmt und den Leiter mitgenommen. Wir anderen mussten unsere Personalien angeben und wurden belehrt, dass ein Strafverfahren eingeleitet werden könne. Dann sollten wir die Wohnung verlassen. Ich stand mitten in der Nacht auf der Straße, immer noch unter voller Wirkung, ohne zu wissen, wie ich nach Hause komme. Ich bin stundenlang durch fremde Straßen gelaufen und habe mich irgendwann in einer Bushaltestelle hingesetzt, bis es hell wurde. Die Hausfassaden haben sich bewegt, und ich habe mich wie ein Verbrecher gefühlt, der überall gesucht wird.
LSD and then a few balloons of laughing gas. I stood up too fast, fainted and hit my head on a table. Woke up not knowing who or where I was, blood on my face. Scary for an hour.

I want to describe this carefully because I've never read about anyone having exactly this experience.

I booked a 'dark retreat': seven days in total darkness in a small hut in the mountains, with food passed in through a light-tight hatch. The idea, according to the organisers, is that after a few days in the dark the brain begins to produce its own psychedelic states. On top of that, they offered an optional 'plant medicine' on day four, which turned out to be a brew containing harmala alkaloids and DMT-containing bark, an ayahuasca analogue. I'd done ayahuasca twice before with good experiences and I wanted to go deeper. I signed the waiver.

Days one to three were hard but manageable. I lost track of time quickly. I slept and woke at random. I meditated. I began to see coloured lights and shapes, which the organiser said was normal. By day three I was having vivid waking dreams. I heard voices sometimes, mostly my own thoughts, but very loud. I was lonely but also curious.

On day four the brew was passed through the hatch with a small candle, which I was told to blow out after drinking. I drank it and sat in the darkness.

What followed I can only describe as the darkness coming alive. Without any light, the visions had nothing to anchor to. They filled the whole space. I saw the walls of the hut covered in eyes, thousands of them, opening one by one. I heard breathing that wasn't mine. Something sat down next to me on the mattress. I felt the mattress dip. I reached out and there was nothing there, but I felt it lean against me.

Then I lost my body. In the darkness there was no way to check where my hands were, no way to see myself. I felt I had become the darkness itself, an infinite black space, and that there was no hut, no mountain, no world. I had always existed in the dark and the light was the dream. I kept trying to remember a single image from my life, my mother's kitchen, my partner's face, and each time the image was swallowed as soon as it formed.

I don't know how long this lasted. In the dark there's no time. It could have been an hour or twelve. At some point I started screaming, and I realised that nobody could hear me. The hut was far from the main house. The protocol was that you knock three times on the hatch in an emergency. I couldn't find the hatch. I crawled along the walls feeling for it, and the walls seemed to go on forever, corners kept appearing where there shouldn't be corners. I was convinced I was trapped in an infinite maze in the dark, and that I'd die there.

Eventually I found the hatch and knocked. Nothing happened. I knocked again and again until my knuckles bled. I don't know how long it took, but eventually it opened and light came in, just a sliver, and it was like being hit by lightning. The organiser's voice asked if I wanted to end the retreat. I said yes. He said it might be better to 'stay with the process' until morning. I begged. He said he would come back in an hour. He closed the hatch.

That hour was the worst of my life. I sat by the hatch with my hand on it, rocking back and forth, feeling the presence next to me, hearing it breathe.

When he came back he opened the door. The light was blinding. He led me out with a blindfold, because coming into full light suddenly can be harmful, he said. I spent the rest of the day in a room with dim light, alone, still tripping. Every shadow moved. I left the next morning.

Pilze bei Freunden. Ich hatte das Gefühl, dass mein Gesicht schmilzt, und konnte keinen Spiegel mehr ansehen. Ich dachte, dass ich so bleibe und dass jeder sehen kann, wie hässlich ich in Wirklichkeit bin.

I was a child refugee from the war in the Balkans. I came to Germany at seven. I'd done years of therapy and thought I had dealt with it. I did an MDMA-assisted session with a therapist who works underground, because legal options didn't exist where I live. The MDMA made me feel safe and open, and we talked about my childhood. Then, unexpectedly, I was back in the basement in my hometown where we hid during the shelling. I could hear the explosions, smell the damp concrete and the fear of the adults. I saw my mother's face lit by a candle, trying to smile at me. I was seven again and terrified. I started shaking and crying and crawled under the therapist's desk, which felt like the basement. She stayed calm and sat on the floor next to me and talked to me in a soft voice for a long time. I sobbed like I had never sobbed before. At some point, I came out from under the desk and she hugged me. It was terrifying and yet also something I had needed for thirty years.
